translationRepairs: In the fourth month Minister of Education Lu Fafa surrendered Yingzhou to Qi; Jiangzhou inspector Hou Tian was sent against him.
In the fourth month Minister of Education Lu Fahe surrendered Yingzhou to Qi; Jiangzhou inspector Hou Tian was sent against him.
s0004 names 陸法和; 法和 is Fahe, so Lu Fafa is a romanization error and Lu Fahe is the correct replacement.
In the fourth month, Minister of Education Lu Fafa attached Yingzhou to Qi; they sent Jiangzhou Inspector Hou Tian to suppress him.
In the fourth month, Minister of Education Lu Fahe attached Yingzhou to Qi; they sent Jiangzhou Inspector Hou Tian to suppress him.
The same unit’s 陸法和 must be romanized Lu Fahe in the literal field; Fafa misreads 和.
On wuwu his birth mother, Consort Xia Gui, was honored as empress dowager.
On wuwu his birth mother, Worthy Consort Xia, was honored as empress dowager.
s0022’s 夏貴妃 is surname Xia plus the consort rank 貴妃 (Worthy Consort), not a given name Gui; Worthy Consort Xia matches the title formula.
On wuwu his birth mother Consort Xia Gui was honored as empress dowager.
On wuwu his birth mother Worthy Consort Xia was honored as empress dowager.
Literal likewise mistook 貴妃 for a personal name; replacing Consort Xia Gui with Worthy Consort Xia restores the rank title.
Hou, son of former Yong'an marquis Que, succeeded as Prince of Shaoling to serve Empress Hou.
Hou, son of former Yong'an marquis Que, succeeded as Prince of Shaoling to attend upon the consort of Prince Xie.
s0038 ends 奉攜王后: 攜王 is Prince Xie and 后 his consort, not an Empress Hou; the repair correctly has him attend that consort.
The former Marquis of Yong'an Que's son Hou succeeded to enfeoffment as Prince of Shaoling, attending upon Empress Hou of Emperor Xie.
The former Marquis of Yong'an Que's son Hou succeeded to enfeoffment as Prince of Shaoling, attending upon the consort of Prince Xie.
Literal’s Empress Hou of Emperor Xie invents an empress and misreads 攜王; consort of Prince Xie is the source-supported reading.
East Yangzhou inspector Zhang Biao besieged Taizhou administrator Wang Huaizhen at Yan Rock.
East Yangzhou inspector Zhang Biao besieged Linhai administrator Wang Huaizhen at Yan Rock.
s0041 has 臨海太守; 臨海 is Linhai, not the modern/anachronistic Taizhou.
East Yangzhou Inspector Zhang Biao besieged Taizhou Administrator Wang Huaizhen at Yan Rock.
East Yangzhou Inspector Zhang Biao besieged Linhai Administrator Wang Huaizhen at Yan Rock.
The literal field repeats Taizhou for 臨海; Linhai Administrator is the accurate place-title pairing.
Central Guard General Prince Dakuen of Linchuan received a gate equal to the Three Excellencies at his existing rank; Central Protector Prince Dacheng of Guiyang became Protector-General of the Army.
Central Guard General Prince Dakuan of Linchuan received a gate equal to the Three Excellencies at his existing rank; Central Protector Prince Dacheng of Guiyang became Protector-General of the Army.
s0044’s 大款 is Dakuan; Dakuen is a misromanization of 款.
On jiawu former Shouchang magistrate Liu Rui was made Prince of Yiyin; former Pacify West legal bureau acting staff officer Xiao Hong was made Prince of Baling to attend the Song and Qi empresses.
On jiawu former Shouchang magistrate Liu Rui was made Prince of Ruyin; former Pacify West legal bureau acting staff officer Xiao Dan was made Prince of Baling to attend the Song and Qi empresses.
s0072 has 汝陰王 and 蕭紞: 汝陰 is Ruyin (not Yiyin), and 紞 is Dan (not Hong); both proposed name fixes match the Chinese.

On jiawu former Shouchang magistrate Liu Rui was made Prince of Yiyin; former Pacify West legal bureau acting staff officer Xiao Hong was made Prince of Baling, attending upon the empresses of Song and Qi.

On jiawu former Shouchang magistrate Liu Rui was made Prince of Ruyin; former Pacify West legal bureau acting staff officer Xiao Dan was made Prince of Baling, attending upon the empresses of Song and Qi.
Literal carries the same two errors; Ruyin and Xiao Dan are required by 汝陰 and 蕭紞.

Xiao Zi and Yu Xiaoqing's armies withdrew and fled.

The historical minister, Attendant-in-Ordinary and Duke of Zheng Wei Zheng, said, "The High Ancestor was indeed one whom Heaven let range freely: intelligent and versed in antiquity, his Way nearly matched innate knowledge; his learning made him broadly informed, truly civil and martial, accomplished in many arts and talents.

The historiographer, Attendant-in-Ordinary and Duke of Zheng Wei Zheng, said, "The High Ancestor was indeed one whom Heaven let range freely: intelligent and versed in antiquity, his Way nearly matched innate knowledge; his learning made him broadly informed, truly civil and martial, accomplished in many arts and talents.
s0139 opens 史臣侍中; 史臣 is the historiographer’s voice (as in adjacent 史臣曰), not ‘historical minister’.

He said Zhou could be punished; allies assembled unlooked-for; he leapt like a dragon at Fan and Han and struck like lightning at Xiang and Ying; cutting Li was like shaking dry stalks; taking the lone tyrant was like picking up what was lost.

He said Zhou could be punished; allies assembled unlooked-for; he leapt like a dragon at Fan and Han and struck like lightning at Xiang and Ying; cutting down those of alienated virtue was like shaking dry stalks; taking the lone tyrant was like picking up what was lost.
剪離德 is ‘cut down those of alienated virtue,’ not a person Li; the proposed idiomatic removes the invented name and restores the parallel with 取獨夫.

Emperor Jing met with an unpropitious house and inherited this time of hardship; campaigns issued from elsewhere and government and punishment were not in his own hands; at the time there were no Yi and Huo to assist him—how could he not yield the throne high?"

Emperor Jing encountered disaster in his ruling house and inherited these troubled times. Military campaigns were directed by others, and neither government nor punishment lay in his own hands. With no Yi Yin or Huo Guang to support him, how could he have avoided the lofty act of yielding the throne?"

The Chinese predicates external control over military, government, and punishment before asking how Emperor Jing could avoid 高讓. The proposal restores grammatical English and correctly expands the conventional Yi Yin and Huo Guang pairing.

Emperor Jing met an unpropitious house and inherited hardship; campaigns issued elsewhere and government and punishment were not his own; with no Yi and Huo to assist, how could he not yield the throne high?"

Emperor Jing inherited a dynasty in ruin and an age of upheaval. Armies marched at another’s command, and neither government nor justice was his to direct. With no Yi Yin or Huo Guang to support him, how could he have avoided yielding the throne?"

The idiomatic revision accurately renders the loss of independent command and government, identifies the paired regent allusion, and expresses 高讓 as yielding the throne rather than the nonsensical phrase 'yield the throne high.'
